You can instruct Amazon S3 to transition objects to less-expensive\\nstorage classes or to archive or delete objects.\\n\\nUse this page to see the scope of the selected S3 Lifecycle rule. An expired object delete marker occurs when all object versions are\\n deleted, and only a single delete marker remains. If you selected this option in\\n your lifecycle rule, an expired object delete marker will be deleted.\\n* You can also see if your lifecycle rule deletes incomplete multipart uploads after\\n a specified number of days\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-view-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Create lifecycle rule\",\"context\":\"# Create lifecycle rule\\n\\nAn Amazon S3 Lifecycle rule configures predefined actions to perform on objects during\\ntheir lifetime. You can create a lifecycle rule to optimize your objects' storage\\ncosts throughout their lifetime.\\n\\nYou can define the scope of the lifecycle rule to all objects in your bucket or to\\nobjects\\nwith a shared prefix, certain object tags, or a certain object size.\\n\\nYou can specify one or more predefined actions for Amazon S3 to perform. There are\\ntwo types of\\nactions: *transition* and *expiration*. Transition actions define when objects transition to a storage\\nclass for less-frequently accessed objects. Expiration actions define when objects\\nare\\nremoved. The effect of these actions depends on the versioning state of your bucket\\nand\\nobjects. Transitions and expirations are asynchronous operations. Your S3 costs, however,\\nare updated as though transitions and expirations were immediate.\\n\\nAmazon S3 has a list of supported lifecycle transitions between storage classes. For\\nmore\\ninformation about which storage classes you can transition objects to and the constraints\\nof\\nobject size, minimum days, and cost considerations, see Supported transitions and related constraints.\\n\\nWhen you create a new S3 Lifecycle rule Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to your\\nLifecycle configuration that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned.\\nYou can allow smaller objects to transition by adding an **Object size** filter that specifies a smaller size to each applicable rule. Additionally, you can\\nchange the default transition behavior so that objects smaller than 128 KB will transition\\nto S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive. To do this, use the\\noptional `x-amz-transition-object-size-minimum-default` header in a PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration request.\\n\\nThe effects of expiration actions are permanent. To prevent accidental deletion, we\\nrecommend that you take precautions, such as enabling S3 Versioning, S3 Object Lock, multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete, or S3 Replication.\\n\\nUnder **Review transition and expiration actions**, you can also review how the specified actions work on the lifecycle of\\ncurrent and noncurrent versions of objects.\\n\\nThere are per-request transition charges to move data into any supported S3 storage\\nclass\\nand charges to store the transitioned objects in the storage class. For details on\\npricing,\\nsee **Lifecycle Transition requests** pricing on the **Requests\\n& data retrievals** tab and **Storage pricing** on the\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-create-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Using Amazon S3 Storage Lens to optimize your storage costs\",\"context\":\"### Step 3: Add lifecycle rules to transition or expire noncurrent object versions\\n\\nAfter you've determined which buckets require further investigation, you can\\nnavigate to the buckets within the S3 console and add a lifecycle rule to expire\\nnoncurrent versions after a specified number of days. Alternatively, to reduce costs\\nwhile still retaining noncurrent versions, you can configure a lifecycle rule to\\ntransition noncurrent versions to one of the Amazon Glacier storage classes. For\\nmore information, see Specifying a lifecycle rule for a versioning-enabled bucket\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-lens-optimize-storage.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Look up S3 lifecycle cost optimization docs"}

{"id": "b68c30ae-489f-4834-8cde-0c0acfffa11d", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Lifecycle rules cut S3 cost by moving data to cheaper storage classes as it ages and by deleting data you no longer need. These are the options that save the most, roughly in order of payoff.

## 1. Clean up waste first
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads.** Add a rule that stops uploads that haven't finished after a set number of days (7 is common). Abandoned parts keep billing and are invisible in normal listings.
- **Expire noncurrent versions.** On versioned buckets, old versions pile up quietly. Delete them after N days, and optionally keep the newest few versions.
- **Remove expired delete markers.** These are leftover markers where every version of the object is already gone.
- **Expire temporary data.** Logs, build artifacts, exports, and scratch data usually have a known shelf life. Scope these rules by prefix or tag.

## 2. Transition data as it ages
Set transitions by object age, using a prefix, tag, or size filter to scope each rule. Typical patterns:
- **Unknown or changing access patterns:** transition to **S3 Intelligent-Tiering**. It moves objects between tiers automatically and has no retrieval fees.
- **Infrequent but needed quickly:** **Standard-IA** or **One Zone-IA**. One Zone-IA is only suitable for re-creatable data.
- **Archive:** **Glacier Instant Retrieval** for millisecond access, **Glacier Flexible Retrieval** for minutes to hours, and **Glacier Deep Archive** for the lowest cost on long-term compliance data.

You can apply the same transitions to noncurrent versions. You can also retain the data and still save money by moving noncurrent versions to a Glacier class instead of deleting them.

## 3. Gotchas that can raise your bill
- **Small objects:** by default, objects under **128 KB** aren't transitioned. This protects you, because per-object transition and minimum-size charges can outweigh the savings. You can override this with an object size filter.
- **Request charges:** each transition costs a per-request fee. Transitioning millions of tiny objects can cost more than it saves.
- **Minimum storage durations:** the IA and Glacier classes bill a minimum duration, such as 30, 90, or 180 days. Deleting or transitioning an object before then still bills for the full period. Check the current constraints in the "Supported transitions and related constraints" page before picking day counts.
- **Retrieval fees:** archiving data you actually read often can cost more than leaving it in Standard.
- **Expiration is permanent.** Consider S3 Versioning, Object Lock, MFA delete, or replication as a safety net, and test rules on a narrow prefix first.
- **Timing:** transitions and expirations run asynchronously, but your billing is updated as though they happened immediately.

## 4. Find where to apply rules
- **S3 Storage Lens** shows which buckets have large amounts of noncurrent-version bytes and incomplete multipart uploads. Those are usually the quickest wins.
- **Storage Class Analysis** and **Cost Explorer** (grouped by usage type) help you choose the age thresholds.

## Example rule set for a versioned bucket
| Rule | Scope | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Abort multipart | Whole bucket | Abort incomplete uploads after 7 days |
| Logs | `logs/` prefix | Transition to Standard-IA at 30 days, Glacier at 90 days, expire at 365 days |
| Old versions | Whole bucket | Move noncurrent versions to Glacier at 30 days, delete at 180 days, keep the newest 3 |
| Cleanup | Whole bucket | Remove expired delete markers |

I can review the buckets in your connected AWS accounts. That would cover which have versioning on, which have no lifecycle configuration, and which have large noncurrent-version or multipart-upload footprints. Tell me which account or region to look at, and whether any buckets have retention or compliance requirements.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
